title: Green Crackers Split Opinion as Delhi Wakes to Severe Post-Diwali Smog
excerpt: The Supreme Court allowed certified green crackers in short windows this Diwali. The science says they pollute less, not nothing — and Delhi's AQI still crossed 350 on Monday morning.
body:
• Delhi woke on Monday, November 9, to air quality index readings above 350, in the severe category, after Diwali firecrackers were set off across the capital on Sunday night despite restrictions.
  • India's Supreme Court allowed only approved green crackers, in set time windows on Saturday and Sunday; green crackers emit less pollution than conventional ones but are not pollution-free, studies cited in reporting show.
  • The divide is structural: vehicles account for 23% of Delhi's winter pollution and biomass burning for 20%, according to figures from India's environment ministry — crackers are one night's spike on a season-long problem.
  • Health experts quoted in coverage called the official response temporary and urged action beyond the festival week.

A thick blanket of smog settled over New Delhi on Monday morning after a Diwali night of firecrackers, pushing the air quality index above 350 in several parts of the capital — the severe category — and reopening India's annual argument over whether the festival of lights can keep its noise and smoke.

The rules this year

Delhi has barred the manufacture, storage, sale and use of firecrackers year-round since January 1, 2025. For this Diwali, the Supreme Court eased the ban slightly: green crackers certified by CSIR-NEERI could be used on November 7 and 8 only, in windows of 6 to 7 a.m. and 8 to 10 p.m., with every box carrying a QR code, while barium-based crackers and joined firecracker strings remained banned outright. Despite the restrictions, residents set off firecrackers through Sunday evening, wire reports from the capital said.

Are green crackers actually green?

Green crackers are formulations developed by the government laboratory CSIR-NEERI to cut emissions — reporting on the science puts the reduction at roughly 15 to 30% for particulate matter against conventional crackers, with barium, lithium, mercury, arsenic and cadmium excluded from their manufacture. Lower is not zero. A Delhi Technological University study cited in coverage found that green crackers also release ultrafine particles that can travel deep into the lungs, and a Central Pollution Control Board study found higher levels of barium and strontium in people's urine after the festival. Around Diwali, hospital cases of wheezing, chest infections, asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease rise by 30 to 40%, health reporting on the festival notes.

The other side of the argument

Defenders of the tradition make two points that the data partly supports. First, crackers are a one-night source: figures from India's Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change attribute 23% of Delhi's winter pollution to vehicles and 20% to biomass burning, including farm stubble fires in Punjab and Haryana, while cooler temperatures and stagnant air trap whatever is emitted. Second, the cracker industry supports manufacturing towns such as Sivakasi, and a ban that is widely flouted, supporters argue, produces the pollution without the compliance. Critics answer that a severe-AQI morning is a health cost imposed on everyone, including people who lit nothing.

"Knee-jerk" and "temporary."

— Shweta Narayan, public health expert at the Global Climate and Health Alliance, describing the government's response, in Press Association coverage

What happens next

The full Delhi ban resumed on November 9, and the argument now moves back to enforcement and to the winter measures — construction limits and diesel-generator restrictions — that authorities apply as pollution season deepens. The structural question the Diwali divide keeps exposing is unchanged: Delhi's air was already more than 30 times the World Health Organization's recommended daily limit on the Wednesday before Diwali, before a single festival cracker was lit.
